1 · Problem

Same stock, different outcome: allocation is the decision

  • A warehouse rarely has enough to cover every store. Every unit sent to one store is a unit another store doesn't get.
  • The decision is a whole number of units per store, under warehouse supply, shelf space and per-item caps.
  • The same 60 units can fulfil 20% more units of demand than an equal split, with no extra warehouse stock.
40 / 20 is one optimal allocation in this simplified illustration, not necessarily the unique optimum. Assumes known demand and identical unit economics.
Interview case study · Walmart M5 sales proxy · synthetic MU economics3 / 18
1 · Problem

Prediction errors and inventory decisions have different costs

  • Synthetic unit economics: 6.00 MU shortage penalty, 1.00 MU holding cost and 0.25 MU shipping cost.
  • Shipping a needed unit saves 5.75 MU net; shipping an unnecessary unit costs 1.25 MU. Allocation mistakes are asymmetric.
  • Compare decisions by realized inventory cost and regret versus hindsight, not forecast error alone.
These are marginal allocation economics, not penalties applied to forecast errors. Costs are simulated, not actual retailer rates.
SHIP ONE MORE UNIT · UNIT IS NEEDED−5.75 MU

6.00 MU shortage avoided − 0.25 MU shipping paid

Reduces total modeled cost
SHIP ONE MORE UNIT · UNIT IS NOT NEEDED+1.25 MU

1.00 MU holding cost + 0.25 MU shipping cost

Increases total modeled cost
The value of a marginal shipment depends on whether demand needs it—and on shared supply constraints.

2 · Approach

Data: what is observed, and what is modeled?

Observed data · Walmart M5

  • Historical daily sales, calendar, prices, store and product identifiers.
  • 5 stores × 10 HOUSEHOLD products per cohort.
  • Two demand regimes: regular and intermittent sellers.
  • Weekly decision origins; sales used as a proxy for demand.

Explicit simulation assumptions

  • Available warehouse stock and store shelf capacities.
  • Shortage, holding and distribution unit costs.
  • Shipment caps and replenishment lead times.
  • MU is synthetic—none of the reported cost differences is actual RM savings.
100 training
8 validation
12 test
Chronological weekly origins; visual segment widths are schematic. The corrected v2 test is retrospective, not a fresh untouched confirmation.
Key limitation: sales can understate underlying demand when products stock out. Actual stock balances are needed for production calibration.
2 · Approach

From history to shipments, with the optimiser in the training loop

Forecast → optimise

Train the forecaster for calibrated probabilities, then optimise. The standard approach and a fair baseline.

Decision-focused learning (DFL)

A surrogate for downstream allocation regret (SPO+) contributes training gradients alongside likelihood.

Same model, same budget

Both versions share architecture, initial weights, data order and epochs. Only the training signal differs.

Interview case study · Walmart M5 sales proxy · synthetic MU economics6 / 18
2 · Approach

DRO: balance expected cost against expensive demand scenarios

  • Simulate many possible next weeks from the forecast, keeping stores' tendency to move together.
  • The robust optimiser gives extra weight to the most expensive scenarios. Mathematically, this equals minimising the average cost of the worst tail of outcomes (CVaR).
  • Two dials: how far into the tail (α) and how much to care about it (risk weight). Both chosen on validation data only: α = 0.75, weight = 0.25.
  • Setting the risk weight to zero gives back the ordinary average-cost plan, a built-in sanity check.
Average-cost plan
every scenario counts equally
Robust plan
expensive scenarios weighted up
Risk protection is conditional: an adverse-scenario hedge can raise average cost when forecast uncertainty is inaccurate or severe demand does not occur.
This is probability-reweighting robustness. It is not Wasserstein DRO, and I label it that way.

How I made the comparison fair

Same conditions

Every policy faces the same weeks, stock, supply, shelf limits and costs.

Two regimes

Strong baselines

Equal split and a proportional rule (last 8 weeks of sales), as a retailer would use.

Checked independently

What changes in multi-period planning?

  • Unsold inventory carries into the next week.
  • Shipments can be in transit when demand arrives.
  • Admission and deferral respect store capacity.
  • Hindsight oracle uses the same physical state transitions.
DFL+PTO vs supervised PTO · 1-week lead1.42% lowerObserved in this test, not established as reliable superiority
Interpretation: DFL + nominal PTO is the lowest-cost non-oracle policy in these regular-demand carryover tests. Intermittent carryover instead favors supervised PTO. These are exploratory, retrospective results.
4 · Solution / Recommendation

Which inventory policy would I recommend to the business?

Operating conditionEvidence from the prototypeRecommendation
Regular demand, one weekProportional baseline lowest cost across three seedsStart with proportional allocation
Intermittent demandPrimary-seed model advantage disappears on retrainingKeep baseline; shadow-test challengers
Repeated replenishmentDFL + PTO lowest observed regular-demand carryover costPilot DFL as a challenger only
High service requirementsCost minimum may fail required fill ratesEnforce service targets; report infeasibility
High business tail riskCost–risk trade-off depends on calibrated scenariosAssess DRO versus a business risk budget
Decision rule: choose the simplest feasible policy that meets cost, service and risk objectives. Promote complexity only after an untouched test shows a meaningful gain.

5 · Impact

Evidence supports a smarter baseline—not guaranteed advanced-model savings

Supported

  • The proportional rule beats equal split by about 133 MU/week (9.3%) in this regular-demand simulation.
  • An open-source integer optimiser handles the constraints in a fraction of a second per week.
  • The evaluation harness catches lucky results: paired intervals, retrained seeds, independent recomputation.

Not supported (yet)

  • That decision-focused learning or robust optimisation beats a simple rule on this data.
  • Any real saving in RM: costs are synthetic and sales stand in for demand.
  • Performance at network scale: this is 5 stores × 10 items per regime.
Recommended business decision: operationalize a strong, auditable baseline first; treat DFL and DRO as research challengers until an untouched real-data comparison demonstrates value.

5 · Impact

A controlled path from prototype to retail pilot

Phase 1 · Shadow
Weeks 1–8

Connect actual stock, sales and unit economics. Run recommendations next to planners without executing orders. Measure feasibility, calibration and modeled decision gaps.

Go if: clear, significant gain vs current practice
Phase 2 · Pilot
Weeks 9–16

Small store/SKU cluster. Compare with the current process under a controlled design; let planners override and record every intervention.

Go if: fewer stockouts, no rise in overstock
Phase 3 · Scale
After pilot review

Scale only after validated pilots; use sparse joint capacity-aware optimization or tested decomposition, with performance and drift monitoring.

Challenger models promoted only on evidence

B1 · The optimisation model

Cost for one week (per store s, item p)
cost = Σ b · shortagesp + h · leftoversp + t · shippedsp
shortage = max(D − I − x, 0) leftover = max(I + x − D, 0)
Constraints
Σs xsp ≤ Wp (warehouse) Σp (Isp + xsp) ≤ Cs (store space) 0 ≤ xsp ≤ Ksp, integer
Value of the k-th extra unit (exact identity, unit-tested)
Marginal shipment cost: t − b if unit prevents shortage; t + h if it stays unsold
expected: ĉ[s,k] = t + h − (b + h) · P(D ≥ I + k)

b = 6.0, h = 1.0, t = 0.25 MU per unit (synthetic). Solver: HiGHS (open source). Fulfilment is recomputed after solving as min(demand, stock).

Interview case study · Walmart M5 sales proxy · synthetic MU economicsBackup

B2 · Decision-focused learning details

SPO+ loss (Elmachtoub & Grigas), used via PyEPO
L(ĉ, c) = maxw∈S (c − 2ĉ)ᵀw + 2ĉᵀw*(c) − c ᵀw*(c)
Training objective
loss = NLL(demand distribution) + λ · SPO+, λ chosen on validation from {0, 0.5, 1, 2}
  • Training uses a fixed set of constraints per item, so SPO+'s assumptions hold. Real weekly limits are applied at decision time.
  • Gradient check: SPO+ gradient is finite and non-zero; λ = 0 vs λ > 0 produce different updates.
  • Validation regret is recomputed after restoring the best checkpoint and calibration.

B3 · Why the robust model equals CVaR

Ambiguity set over N scenarios with base probabilities p
Pα = { w : Σ wj = 1, 0 ≤ wj ≤ pj / (1 − α) }
maxw∈Pα Σ wj Lj(x) = CVaRα(L(x))
Objective
min (1 − ρ) · E[L(x)] + ρ · CVaRα(L(x))
  • Solved exactly as one integer program with the standard CVaR linearisation (η, zj).
  • Checked against brute-force enumeration on small cases; α = 0 or ρ = 0 recovers the average-cost plan.
  • Scenarios share random numbers across policies and keep cross-store dependence learned from training weeks only.
